source: Spiral, elliptical and irregular galaxies differ in shape, gas and the ages of their stars.
Students think every galaxy is a spiral like ours.

Beyond the Milky Way lie hundreds of billions of other galaxies. In 1926 Edwin Hubble sorted the ones he could see by shape, and his scheme is still used. Shape turns out to tell a lot about a galaxy's gas, its stars and its history.

A galaxy's colors come from its stars. Hot, massive blue stars live only a few million years, so a galaxy that looks blue must be making new stars, which needs gas. Spiral arms and irregulars are full of gas and glow with young blue stars and pink nebulae. Ellipticals have used up or lost their gas long ago; with no new stars, only long-lived red and yellow stars remain, so they look reddish. Many large ellipticals are thought to have grown through mergers of smaller galaxies, which scrambles orderly disks into rounded swarms.

Galaxies come as ellipticals (smooth, old red stars, little gas), spirals and barred spirals (disks with arms, gas and young blue stars) and irregulars (no clear shape, gas-rich). The Milky Way is a barred spiral.
Hubble's classes: round and flattened ellipticals, a spiral, a barred spiral, an open spiral and an irregular galaxy (sketches).

Pictures of galaxies tend to show beautiful spirals, so many people think every galaxy is a spiral like ours. Ellipticals are common, especially in crowded clusters of galaxies, and small dwarf galaxies, mostly faint ellipticals and irregulars, are the most numerous of all. Check: our own neighborhood, the Local Group, has three big spirals (the Milky Way, Andromeda and Triangulum) and dozens of dwarfs.
